In what, then, does the difference between such a fiction and a belief consist? It does not lie merely in some peculiar idea attached to a conception that compels our assent and is missing in every known fiction. For since the mind has authority over all its ideas, it could voluntarily attach this particular idea to any fiction, and consequently be able to believe whatever it pleases — contrary to what we find in daily experience. We can, in our conception, join the head of a man to the body of a horse; but it is not in our power to believe that such an animal has ever really existed.

It follows, then, that the difference between _fiction_ and _belief_ lies in some sentiment or feeling attached to the latter, not to the former, which does not depend on the will, and cannot be commanded at pleasure. It must be aroused by nature, like all other sentiments, and must arise from the particular situation in which the mind is placed at any particular moment. Whenever an object is presented to the memory or senses, it immediately, by the force of custom, carries the imagination to conceive the object usually conjoined with it; and this conception is attended by a feeling or sentiment, different from the loose reveries of fancy. In this consists the whole nature of belief. For since there is no matter of fact we believe so firmly that we cannot conceive its contrary, there would be no difference between the conception assented to and that which is rejected, were it not for some sentiment that distinguishes the one from the other. If I see a billiard ball moving toward another on a smooth table, I can easily conceive its stopping on contact. This conception implies no contradiction; but still it feels very differently from the conception by which I represent to myself the impact and the transfer of motion from one ball to another.

40. Were we to attempt a _definition_ of this sentiment, we should perhaps find it a very difficult, if not impossible, task — just as if we should try to define the feeling of cold or the passion of anger to a creature who had never experienced these sentiments. Belief is the true and proper name of this feeling, and no one is ever at a loss for the meaning of that term, because every man is at every moment conscious of the sentiment it represents. It may not, however, be improper to attempt a _description_ of this sentiment, in the hope that by this means we may arrive at some analogies that may provide a more complete account of it. I say, then, that belief is nothing but a more vivid, lively, forceful, firm, and steady conception of an object than the imagination alone is ever able to attain. This variety of terms, which may seem so unphilosophical, is meant only to express that act of the mind which makes realities, or what is taken for such, more present to us than fictions, causes them to weigh more in thought, and gives them a superior influence on the passions and imagination. As long as we agree about the thing, it is pointless to dispute about the terms. The imagination has command over all its ideas, and can join and mix and vary them in every possible way. It may conceive fictitious objects with every circumstance of place and time. It may set them, as it were, before our eyes in their true colors, just as they might have existed. But since it is impossible that this faculty of imagination can ever, of itself, reach belief, it is evident that belief consists not in the peculiar nature or order of ideas, but in the _manner_ of their conception, and in their _feeling_ to the mind. I admit that it is impossible to explain this feeling or manner of conception perfectly. We may use words that express something close to it. But its true and proper name, as we observed before, is _belief_, a term that everyone sufficiently understands in common life. And in philosophy we can go no further than to assert that _belief_ is something felt by the mind, which distinguishes the ideas of judgment from the fictions of imagination. It gives them more weight and influence; makes them appear of greater importance; impresses them on the mind; and makes them the governing principle of our actions. Right now, for instance, I hear the voice of a person I know, and the sound comes as from the next room. This impression on my senses immediately carries my thought to the person, together with all the surrounding objects. I paint them out to myself as existing now, with the same qualities and relations I formerly knew them to possess. These ideas take a firmer hold on my mind than ideas of an enchanted castle. They have a very different feel, and a far greater influence of every kind, in giving either pleasure or pain, joy or sorrow.

Let us, then, take in the whole scope of this doctrine, and grant that the sentiment of belief is nothing but a conception more intense and steady than that which attends the mere fictions of imagination, and that this _manner_ of conception arises from a customary conjunction of the object with something present to the memory or senses. On these suppositions, I believe it will not be difficult to find other operations of the mind analogous to it, and to trace these phenomena to principles still more general.

41. We have already observed that nature has established connections among particular ideas, and that no sooner does one idea occur to our thoughts than it introduces its correlative and carries our attention toward it by a gentle and imperceptible movement. These principles of connection or association we have reduced to three, namely: _Resemblance_, _Contiguity_, and _Causation_, which are the only bonds that unite our thoughts together and produce that regular train of reflection or discourse which, in greater or lesser degree, takes place among all mankind. Now here arises a question on which the solution of the present difficulty will depend. Does it happen, in all these relations, that when one of the objects is presented to the senses or memory, the mind is not only carried to the conception of the correlative, but reaches a steadier and stronger conception of it than it would otherwise have been able to attain? This seems to be the case with the belief that arises from the relation of cause and effect. And if the case is the same with the other relations or principles of association, this may be established as a general law governing all the operations of the mind.

We may therefore observe, as the first experiment for our present purpose, that, on seeing the picture of an absent friend, our idea of him is evidently enlivened by the _resemblance_, and every passion which that idea occasions, whether of joy or sorrow, gains new force and vigor. In producing this effect, both a relation and a present impression concur. Where the picture bears him no resemblance, or at least was not intended for him, it does not even carry our thought to him; and when the picture is absent, as well as the person, though the mind may pass from the thought of the one to that of the other, it feels its idea rather weakened than enlivened by that transition. We take pleasure in viewing the picture of a friend when it is set before us; but when it is removed, we would rather think of him directly than through reflection in an image equally distant and obscure.

The ceremonies of the Roman Catholic religion may be considered as instances of the same kind. The devotees of that religion usually plead in excuse for the rituals with which they are reproached that they feel the good effect of those outward motions, postures, and actions in enlivening their devotion and quickening their fervor, which would otherwise decay if directed entirely to distant and immaterial objects. We shadow forth the objects of our faith, they say, in sensible types and images, and make them more present to us through the immediate presence of these types than would be possible by purely intellectual view and contemplation. Sensible objects always have a greater influence on the fancy than any others, and this influence they readily convey to the ideas to which they are related and which they resemble. I shall only infer from these practices and this reasoning that the effect of resemblance in enlivening ideas is very common; and since in every such case a resemblance and a present impression must concur, we are abundantly supplied with experiments to prove the reality of the foregoing principle.

42. We may strengthen these experiments by others of a different kind, by considering the effects of _contiguity_ as well as _resemblance_. It is certain that distance lessens the force of every idea, and that, as we approach any object, even before it appears to our senses, it acts on the mind with an influence that imitates an immediate impression. Thinking about any object readily transports the mind to what is nearby; but only the actual presence of an object transports it with greater vividness. When I am a few miles from home, anything relating to home touches me more nearly than when I am two hundred leagues away; though even at that distance, reflecting on anything in the neighborhood of my friends or family naturally produces an idea of them. But since in this latter case both the objects of the mind are ideas, even though there is an easy transition between them, that transition alone is not able to give superior vividness to any of the ideas, for lack of some immediate impression[8].

[8] 'Naturane nobis, inquit, datum dicam, an errore quodam, ut, cum ea loca videamus, in quibus memoria dignos viros acceperimus multum esse versatos, magis moveamur, quam siquando eorum ipsorum aut facta audiamus aut scriptum aliquod legamus? Velut ego nunc moveor. Venit enim mihi Plato in mentem, quera accepimus primum hic disputare solitum: cuius etiam illi hortuli propinqui non memoriam solum mihi afferunt, sed ipsum videntur in conspectu meo hic ponere. Hic Speusippus, hic Xenocrates, hic eius auditor Polemo; cuius ipsa illa sessio fuit, quam videmus. Equidem etiam curiam nostram, Hostiliam dico, non hanc novam, quae mihi minor esse videtur postquam est maior, solebam intuens, Scipionem, Catonem, Laelium, nostrum vero in primis avum cogitare. Tanta vis admonitionis est in locis; ut non sine causa ex his memoriae deducta sit disciplina.'

43. No one can doubt that causation has the same influence as the other two relations of resemblance and contiguity. Superstitious people are fond of the relics of saints and holy men for the same reason that they seek out types or images: to enliven their devotion and give them a more intimate and powerful conception of those exemplary lives which they wish to imitate. Now it is obvious that one of the best relics a devotee could acquire would be the handiwork of a saint; and if his clothes and furniture are ever considered in this light, it is because they were once at his disposal, moved and affected by him — in which respect they are to be considered as imperfect effects, connected to him by a shorter chain of consequences than those by which we know the reality of his existence.

Suppose the son of a friend who has been long dead or absent were brought before us. It is obvious that this object would instantly revive its correlative idea, and recall all past intimacies and familiarities to our thoughts in more lively colors than they would otherwise have appeared. This is another phenomenon that seems to confirm the principle stated above.

44. We may notice that in these phenomena, the belief in the correlative object is always presupposed; without it, the relation could have no effect. The influence of the picture supposes that we _believe_ our friend once existed. Contiguity to home can never excite our ideas of home unless we _believe_ that it really exists. Now I assert that this belief, where it reaches beyond the memory or senses, is of a similar nature, and arises from similar causes, as the transition of thought and vividness of conception just explained. When I throw a piece of dry wood into a fire, my mind is immediately led to conceive that it increases, not extinguishes, the flame. This transition of thought from cause to effect does not proceed from reason. It derives its origin entirely from custom and experience. And since it begins from an object present to the senses, it makes the idea or conception of flame stronger and livelier than any loose, floating reverie of the imagination. That idea arises immediately. The thought moves instantly toward it and conveys to it all the force of conception that derives from the impression present to the senses. When a sword is leveled at my breast, does not the idea of wound and pain strike me more strongly than when a glass of wine is presented to me, even if by accident this idea should occur after the appearance of the latter object? But what is there in this whole matter to produce such a strong conception, except simply a present object and a customary transition to the idea of another object that we have been used to joining with the former? This is the whole operation of the mind in all our conclusions concerning matters of fact and existence; and it is a satisfaction to find some analogies by which it may be explained. The transition from a present object always gives strength and solidity to the related idea.

Here, then, is a kind of pre-established harmony between the course of nature and the succession of our ideas; and though the powers and forces by which nature is governed are wholly unknown to us, yet our thoughts and conceptions have still, we find, run on in the same track as the rest of nature's works. Custom is the principle by which this correspondence has been brought about — so necessary to the survival of our species and the regulation of our conduct in every circumstance and event of human life. Had not the presence of an object instantly excited the idea of those objects commonly conjoined with it, all our knowledge would have been limited to the narrow sphere of memory and senses; and we should never have been able to adjust means to ends, or to employ our natural powers either for the production of good or the avoidance of evil. Those who delight in the discovery and contemplation of _final causes_ have here ample subject to occupy their wonder and admiration.

45. I shall add, by way of further confirmation of the foregoing theory, that since this operation of the mind, by which we infer like effects from like causes, and _vice versa_, is so essential to the survival of all human creatures, it is unlikely that it could be entrusted to the fallible deductions of our reason, which is slow in its operations, does not appear at all during the first years of infancy, and at best is, in every age and period of human life, extremely liable to error and mistake. It is more in keeping with the ordinary wisdom of nature to secure so necessary an act of the mind by some instinct or mechanical tendency that may be infallible in its operations, may show itself at the first appearance of life and thought, and may be independent of all the labored deductions of the understanding. As nature has taught us the use of our limbs without giving us the knowledge of the muscles and nerves by which they are moved, so she has implanted in us an instinct that carries thought forward in a course corresponding to that which she has established among external objects, even though we are ignorant of the powers and forces on which this regular course and succession of objects entirely depends.

chapters.title: Section 6: OF PROBABILITY[9].
paragraphs: [9] Mr. Locke divides all arguments into demonstrative and probable. On this view, we must say that it is only probable that all men must die, or that the sun will rise tomorrow. But to bring our language more in line with common use, we ought to divide arguments into _demonstrations_, _proofs_, and _probabilities_. By proofs I mean such arguments from experience as leave no room for doubt or opposition.

46. Although there is no such thing as _Chance_ in the world, our ignorance of the real cause of any event has the same influence on the understanding, and gives rise to a similar kind of belief or opinion.

There is certainly a probability that arises from a superiority of chances on one side; and as this superiority increases, surpassing the opposite chances, the probability receives a corresponding increase, and gives rise to a still higher degree of belief or assent to the side on which we discover the superiority. If a die were marked with one figure or number of spots on four sides, and another figure or number of spots on the two remaining sides, it would be more probable that the former would turn up than the latter; but if it had a thousand sides marked in the same way, and only one side different, the probability would be much higher, and our belief or expectation of the event more steady and secure. This process of thought or reasoning may seem trivial and obvious; but to those who look at it more closely, it may perhaps provide material for curious speculation.

It seems clear that when the mind looks ahead to discover the event that may result from the throw of such a die, it considers the turning up of each particular side as equally probable; and this is the very nature of chance — to make all the particular events comprehended in it entirely equal. But finding that a greater number of sides agree on one event than on the other, the mind is carried more frequently to that event, and meets it more often as it turns over the various possibilities or chances on which the final result depends. This concurrence of several views on one particular event immediately gives rise, by an inexplicable contrivance of nature, to the sentiment of belief, and gives that event the advantage over its competitor, which is supported by a smaller number of views and recurs less often to the mind. If we grant that belief is nothing but a firmer and stronger conception of an object than what attends the mere fictions of the imagination, this operation may perhaps be accounted for in some measure. The concurrence of these several views or glimpses imprints the idea more strongly on the imagination, gives it greater force and vigor, makes its influence on the passions and affections more perceptible, and, in a word, produces that reliance or security that constitutes the nature of belief and opinion.

47. The case is the same with the probability of causes as with that of chance. There are some causes that are entirely uniform and constant in producing a particular effect, and no instance has yet been found of any failure or irregularity in their operation. Fire has always burned, and water suffocated every human creature. The production of motion by impact and gravity is a universal law that has so far admitted of no exception. But there are other causes that have been found more irregular and uncertain; rhubarb has not always proved a purge, nor opium a sleep-inducer, to everyone who has taken these medicines. It is true that when any cause fails to produce its usual effect, philosophers do not ascribe this to any irregularity in nature; they suppose that some hidden causes, in the particular structure of parts, have prevented the operation. Our reasonings and conclusions about the event, however, are the same as if this principle did not apply. Being determined by custom to transfer the past to the future in all our inferences, where the past has been entirely regular and uniform we expect the event with the greatest assurance and leave no room for any contrary supposition. But where different effects have been found to follow from causes that are to _appearance_ exactly similar, all these various effects must occur to the mind in transferring the past to the future, and enter into our reckoning when we determine the probability of the event. Though we give preference to that which has been found most usual, and believe that this effect will occur, we must not overlook the other effects, but must assign to each of them a particular weight and authority, in proportion to how frequently we have found it to occur. It is more probable, in almost every country in Europe, that there will be frost sometime in January, than that the weather will continue mild throughout that whole month; though this probability varies according to different climates, and approaches certainty in the more northern kingdoms. Here, then, it seems evident that when we transfer the past to the future, in order to determine the effect that will result from any cause, we transfer all the different events in the same proportion as they have appeared in the past, and conceive one to have existed a hundred times, for instance, another ten times, and another once. Since a great number of views here agree on one event, they fortify and confirm it for the imagination, give rise to the sentiment we call _belief_, and give its object the preference over the contrary event, which is not supported by an equal number of experiments and does not recur so frequently to thought in transferring the past to the future. Let anyone try to account for this operation of the mind on any of the received systems of philosophy, and he will be aware of the difficulty. For my part, I shall think it enough if these present hints excite the curiosity of philosophers, and make them aware how defective all common theories are in treating such curious and sublime subjects.

chapters.title: Section 7: OF THE IDEA OF NECESSARY CONNEXION. — Part 1
paragraphs: 48. The great advantage of the mathematical sciences over the moral consists in this: that the ideas of the former, being sensible, are always clear and determinate, the smallest distinction between them is immediately perceptible, and the same terms continue to express the same ideas, without ambiguity or variation. An oval is never mistaken for a circle, nor a hyperbola for an ellipse. The isosceles and the scalene are distinguished by boundaries more exact than vice and virtue, right and wrong. If any term is defined in geometry, the mind readily, of itself, substitutes on all occasions the definition for the term defined; and even where no definition is used, the object itself may be presented to the senses, and by this means be steadily and clearly apprehended. But the finer sentiments of the mind, the operations of the understanding, the various agitations of the passions, though really distinct in themselves, easily escape us when surveyed by reflection; nor is it in our power to recall the original object as often as we have occasion to contemplate it. Ambiguity is thus gradually introduced into our reasonings: similar objects are readily taken to be the same, and the conclusion becomes at last very far from the premises.

One may, however, safely affirm that, if we view these sciences in a proper light, their advantages and disadvantages nearly balance each other and put both of them on an equal footing. If the mind retains the ideas of geometry clear and determinate with greater ease, it must carry on a much longer and more intricate chain of reasoning, and compare ideas much further apart, in order to reach the more abstruse truths of that science. And if moral ideas are apt, without extreme care, to fall into obscurity and confusion, the inferences in such discussions are always much shorter, and the intermediate steps that lead to the conclusion much fewer, than in the sciences that deal with quantity and number. In reality, there is scarcely a proposition in Euclid so simple that it does not consist of more parts than are to be found in any moral reasoning that does not run into chimera and conceit. Where we trace the principles of the human mind through a few steps, we may be quite satisfied with our progress, considering how soon nature blocks all our inquiries into causes and reduces us to acknowledging our ignorance. The chief obstacle, therefore, to our improvement in the moral or metaphysical sciences is the obscurity of the ideas and the ambiguity of the terms. The principal difficulty in mathematics is the length of the inferences and the scope of thought required to reach any conclusion. And perhaps our progress in natural philosophy is chiefly retarded by the lack of proper experiments and phenomena, which are often discovered by chance, and cannot always be found when needed, even by the most diligent and prudent inquiry. Since moral philosophy seems so far to have received less improvement than either geometry or physics, we may conclude that if there is any difference in this respect among these sciences, the difficulties that obstruct the progress of moral philosophy require superior care and capacity to be surmounted.

49. There are no ideas in metaphysics more obscure and uncertain than those of _power, force, energy_, or _necessary connection_, which it is every moment necessary for us to treat in all our discussions. We shall, therefore, try in this section to fix, if possible, the precise meaning of these terms, and thereby remove some of the obscurity so often complained of in this kind of philosophy.

It seems a proposition that will not admit of much dispute, that all our ideas are nothing but copies of our impressions; or, in other words, that it is impossible for us to _think_ of anything we have not previously _felt_, either by our external or internal senses. I have endeavored[10] to explain and prove this proposition, and have expressed my hope that, by a proper application of it, men may reach a greater clarity and precision in philosophical reasoning than they have hitherto been able to attain. Complex ideas may perhaps be well known by definition, which is nothing but an enumeration of those parts or simple ideas that compose them. But when we have pushed definitions up to the most simple ideas, and still find some ambiguity and obscurity, what resource have we then? By what device can we throw light on these ideas, and render them altogether precise and determinate to our intellectual view? Produce the impressions or original sentiments from which the ideas are copied. These impressions are all strong and sensible. They admit of no ambiguity. Not only are they placed in full light themselves, but they may throw light on the corresponding ideas, which lie in obscurity. And by this means, we may perhaps attain a new microscope or kind of optics, by which, in the moral sciences, the most minute and most simple ideas may be so enlarged as to fall readily under our apprehension, and to be known just as well as the grossest and most sensible ideas that can be the object of our inquiry.

50. To be fully acquainted, therefore, with the idea of power or necessary connection, let us examine its impression; and, in order to find the impression with greater certainty, let us search for it in all the sources from which it may possibly be derived.

When we look about us at external objects, and consider the operation of causes, we are never able, in a single instance, to discover any power or necessary connection — any quality that binds the effect to the cause and makes the one an infallible consequence of the other. We only find that the one does in fact follow the other. The impact of one billiard ball is attended with motion in the second. This is the whole of what appears to the _outward_ senses. The mind feels no sentiment or _inward_ impression from this succession of objects. Consequently, there is not, in any single particular instance of cause and effect, anything that can suggest the idea of power or necessary connection.

From the first appearance of an object, we can never conjecture what effect will result from it. But if the power or energy of any cause were discoverable by the mind, we could foresee the effect even without experience, and could from the start pronounce with certainty about it by mere force of thought and reasoning.

In reality, no part of matter ever, by its sensible qualities, reveals any power or energy, or gives us grounds to imagine that it could produce anything, or be followed by any other object we could call its effect. Solidity, extension, motion — these qualities are all complete in themselves and never point to any other event that may result from them. The scenes of the universe are continually shifting, and one object follows another in an uninterrupted succession; but the power or force that drives the whole machine is entirely concealed from us and never reveals itself in any of the sensible qualities of body. We know that, in fact, heat is a constant attendant of flame; but what the connection between them is, we have no room even to guess or imagine. It is therefore impossible that the idea of power can be derived from the contemplation of bodies, in single instances of their operation, because no bodies ever reveal any power that can be the source of this idea.[11]

[11] Mr. Locke, in his chapter on power, says that, finding from experience that there are various new productions in nature, and concluding that there must somewhere be a power capable of producing them, we arrive at last by this reasoning at the idea of power. But no reasoning can ever give us a new, original, simple idea, as this philosopher himself admits. This, therefore, can never be the origin of that idea.

51. Since, then, external objects, as they appear to the senses, give us no idea of power or necessary connection by their operation in particular instances, let us see whether this idea is derived from reflection on the operations of our own minds, and is copied from any internal impression. It may be said that we are at every moment conscious of internal power: while we feel that, by the simple command of our will, we can move the organs of our body or direct the faculties of our mind. An act of volition produces motion in our limbs, or raises a new idea in our imagination. This influence of the will we know by consciousness. Hence we acquire the idea of power or energy, and are certain that we ourselves and all other intelligent beings possess power. This idea, then, is an idea of reflection, since it arises from reflecting on the operations of our own mind, and on the command which the will exerts both over the organs of the body and over the faculties of the soul.

52. We shall proceed to examine this claim, beginning with the influence of volition over the organs of the body. This influence, we may note, is a fact which, like all other natural events, can be known only by experience, and can never be foreseen from any apparent energy or power in the cause that links it to the effect, and makes the one an infallible consequence of the other. The motion of our body follows on the command of our will. Of this we are conscious every moment. But the means by which this is brought about, the energy by which the will performs so extraordinary an operation — of this we are so far from being immediately conscious that it must forever escape our most diligent inquiry.

For _first_: is there any principle in all nature more mysterious than the union of soul with body, by which a supposed spiritual substance acquires such an influence over a material one that the most refined thought is able to move the grossest matter? Were we empowered, by a secret wish, to move mountains or guide the planets in their orbits, this extensive authority would not be more extraordinary, nor more beyond our comprehension. But if we perceived by consciousness any power or energy in the will, we must know this power; we must know its connection with the effect; we must know the hidden union of soul and body and the nature of both these substances, by which the one is able to act, in so many instances, upon the other.

_Secondly_, we are not able to move all the organs of the body with equal authority, though we can give no reason besides experience for so remarkable a difference between one and the other. Why has the will an influence over the tongue and fingers, and not over the heart or liver? This question would never trouble us if we were conscious of a power in the former case and not in the latter. We should then perceive, independently of experience, why the authority of the will over the organs of the body is confined within such particular limits. Being in that case fully acquainted with the power or force by which it operates, we should also know why its influence reaches just to such boundaries and no further.

A man suddenly struck with palsy in his leg or arm, or who has newly lost those limbs, often tries at first to move them and use them in their usual functions. Here he is just as conscious of a power to command such limbs as a man in perfect health is conscious of a power to move any member that remains in its natural state and condition. But consciousness never deceives. Consequently, neither in the one case nor in the other are we ever conscious of any power. We learn the influence of our will from experience alone. And experience only teaches us how one event constantly follows another, without informing us of the hidden connection that binds them together and makes them inseparable.

_Thirdly_, we learn from anatomy that the immediate object of power in voluntary motion is not the limb itself that is moved, but certain muscles, and nerves, and animal spirits, and perhaps something still more minute and unknown, through which the motion is successively propagated before it reaches the limb itself whose motion is the immediate object of volition. Can there be a more certain proof that the power by which this whole operation is performed, far from being directly and fully known by an inward sentiment or consciousness, is mysterious and unintelligible to the last degree? Here the mind wills a certain event: immediately another event, unknown to us and totally different from the one intended, is produced; this event produces another, equally unknown, until at last, through a long succession, the desired event is produced. But if the original power were felt, it must be known; were it known, its effect must also be known, since all power is relative to its effect. And _vice versa_, if the effect is not known, the power cannot be known or felt. Indeed, how can we be conscious of a power to move our limbs, when we have no such power, but only a power to move certain animal spirits which, though they at last produce the motion of our limbs, yet operate in a manner wholly beyond our comprehension?

We may therefore conclude from the whole, I hope without rashness, though with assurance, that our idea of power is not copied from any sentiment or consciousness of power within ourselves, when we give rise to bodily motion, or apply our limbs to their proper use and function. That their motion follows the command of the will is a matter of common experience, like other natural events; but the power or energy by which this is brought about, like that in other natural events, is unknown and inconceivable.[12]

[12] It may be claimed that the resistance we meet with in bodies, which often obliges us to exert our force and call up all our power, gives us the idea of force and power. It is this _nisus_, or strong endeavor, of which we are conscious, that is the original impression from which this idea is copied. But, first, we attribute power to a vast number of objects where we can never suppose this resistance or exertion of force takes place — to the Supreme Being, who never meets with any resistance; to the mind in its command over its ideas and limbs, in ordinary thinking and motion, where the effect follows immediately on the will, without any exertion or summoning up of force; to inanimate matter, which is not capable of this sentiment. _Secondly_, this sentiment of an endeavor to overcome resistance has no known connection with any event: what follows it, we know by experience, but could not know _a priori_. It must be admitted, however, that the animal _nisus_ which we experience, though it can give no accurate or precise idea of power, enters very much into the common, inaccurate idea formed of it.

53. Shall we then assert that we are conscious of a power or energy in our own minds when, by an act or command of our will, we raise up a new idea, fix the mind on the contemplation of it, turn it on all sides, and at last dismiss it for some other idea, when we think we have surveyed it with sufficient accuracy? I believe the same arguments will prove that even this command of the will gives us no real idea of force or energy.

_First_, it must be granted that when we know a power, we know the very feature in the cause by which it is enabled to produce the effect; for these are supposed to be synonymous. We must, therefore, know both the cause and the effect, and the relation between them. But do we pretend to be acquainted with the nature of the human soul and the nature of an idea, or the fitness of the one to produce the other? This is a real creation; a production of something out of nothing — implying a power so great that it may seem, at first sight, beyond the reach of any being less than infinite. At least it must be owned that such a power is not felt, nor known, nor even conceivable by the mind. We only feel the event — namely, the existence of an idea following on a command of the will; but the manner in which this operation is performed, the power by which it is produced, is entirely beyond our comprehension.

_Secondly_, the mind's command over itself is limited, just as its command over the body is; and these limits are not known by reason, or by any acquaintance with the nature of cause and effect, but only by experience and observation, as in all other natural events and in the operation of external objects. Our authority over our sentiments and passions is much weaker than that over our ideas; and even the latter authority is confined within very narrow boundaries. Will anyone pretend to assign the ultimate reason for these boundaries, or show why the power is deficient in one case and not in another?

_Thirdly_, this self-command is very different at different times. A man in health possesses more of it than one languishing with illness. We are more master of our thoughts in the morning than in the evening; fasting, than after a full meal. Can we give any reason for these variations except experience? Where, then, is the power we pretend to be conscious of? Is there not here, either in a spiritual or material substance or both, some hidden mechanism or structure of parts, on which the effect depends, and which, being entirely unknown to us, renders the power or energy of the will equally unknown and incomprehensible?

Volition is surely an act of the mind with which we are sufficiently acquainted. Reflect on it. Consider it from all sides. Do you find anything in it like this creative power by which it raises a new idea out of nothing and, with a kind of _Fiat_, imitates the omnipotence of its Maker (if I may be allowed to put it so) who called forth into existence all the various scenes of nature? So far from being conscious of this energy in the will, it requires as definite an experience as that we have, to convince us that such extraordinary effects ever result from a simple act of volition.

54. Most of mankind never find any difficulty in accounting for the more common and familiar operations of nature — such as the falling of heavy bodies, the growth of plants, the generation of animals, or the nourishment of bodies by food. But they suppose that, in all these cases, they perceive the very force or energy of the cause by which it is connected with its effect, and is forever infallible in its operation. By long habit they acquire such a turn of mind that, on the appearance of the cause, they immediately expect its usual attendant with assurance, and scarcely conceive it possible that any other event could result from it. It is only on the appearance of extraordinary phenomena, such as earthquakes, pestilence, and prodigies of any kind, that they find themselves at a loss to assign a proper cause and to explain how the effect is produced by it. It is usual for men, in such difficulties, to have recourse to some invisible intelligent principle[13] as the immediate cause of the event that surprises them, and which they think cannot be accounted for by the ordinary powers of nature. But philosophers, who carry their scrutiny a little further, immediately see that even in the most familiar events the energy of the cause is as unintelligible as in the most unusual, and that we only learn by experience the frequent _Conjunction_ of objects, without ever being able to comprehend anything like _Connection_ between them.

55. Here, then, many philosophers think themselves obliged by reason to have recourse on all occasions to the same principle to which the common people appeal only in cases that appear miraculous and supernatural. They acknowledge mind and intelligence to be not only the ultimate and original cause of all things, but the immediate and sole cause of every event in nature. They claim that those objects commonly called _causes_ are in reality nothing but _occasions_, and that the true and direct principle of every effect is not any power or force in nature, but a volition of the Supreme Being, who wills that such particular objects should forever be conjoined with each other. Instead of saying that one billiard ball moves another by a force derived from the author of nature, it is the Deity himself, they say, who, by a particular volition, moves the second ball, being determined to this operation by the impact of the first ball, in accordance with those general laws he has laid down for himself in governing the universe. But philosophers, advancing still further in their inquiries, discover that, as we are totally ignorant of the power on which the mutual operation of bodies depends, we are no less ignorant of the power on which depends the operation of mind on body, or of body on mind; nor can we, either from our senses or from consciousness, assign the ultimate principle in one case more than in the other. The same ignorance, therefore, reduces them to the same conclusion. They assert that the Deity is the immediate cause of the union between soul and body; and that it is not the organs of sense which, being agitated by external objects, produce sensations in the mind, but a particular volition of our omnipotent Maker, which excites such a sensation, in consequence of such a motion in the organ. In the same way, it is not any energy in the will that produces local motion in our limbs: it is God himself who is pleased to second our will, in itself impotent, and to command the motion which we erroneously attribute to our own power and efficacy. Nor do philosophers stop at this conclusion. They sometimes extend the same inference to the mind itself, in its internal operations. Our mental vision or conception of ideas is nothing but a revelation made to us by our Maker. When we voluntarily turn our thoughts to any object and raise its image in the fancy, it is not the will that creates that idea: it is the universal Creator who discovers it to the mind and renders it present to us.

56. Thus, according to these philosophers, everything is full of God. Not content with the principle that nothing exists except by his will, that nothing possesses any power except by his concession, they strip nature, and all created beings, of every power, in order to make their dependence on the Deity still more perceptible and immediate. They do not consider that, by this theory, they diminish, instead of magnifying, the grandeur of the attributes they so much affect to celebrate. It surely argues more power in the Deity to delegate a certain degree of power to inferior creatures, than to produce everything by his own immediate volition. It argues more wisdom to design from the start the fabric of the world with such perfect foresight that, of itself, and by its proper operation, it may serve all the purposes of providence, than if the great Creator had to adjust its parts every moment, and animate by his breath all the wheels of that stupendous machine.
But if we want a more philosophical refutation of this theory, perhaps the following two reflections will suffice.

57. _First_, it seems to me that this theory of the universal energy and operation of the Supreme Being is too bold ever to carry conviction with a man sufficiently aware of the weakness of human reason and the narrow limits to which it is confined in all its operations. Even if the chain of arguments leading to it were ever so logical, a strong suspicion must arise — if not an absolute assurance — that it has carried us quite beyond the reach of our faculties, when it leads to conclusions so extraordinary and so remote from common life and experience. We are in fairy land long before we have reached the final steps of our theory; and _there_ we have no reason to trust our common methods of argument, or to think that our usual analogies and probabilities have any authority. Our line is too short to fathom such immense abysses. And however we may flatter ourselves that we are guided, in every step we take, by a kind of verisimilitude and experience, we may be sure that this fancied experience has no authority when we thus apply it to subjects that lie entirely outside the sphere of experience. But on this we shall have occasion to touch afterwards.[14]

_Secondly_, I cannot see any force in the arguments on which this theory is founded. We are ignorant, it is true, of the manner in which bodies operate on each other: their force or energy is entirely incomprehensible. But are we not equally ignorant of the manner or force by which a mind — even the supreme mind — operates either on itself or on body? Where, I ask, do we acquire any idea of it? We have no sentiment or consciousness of this power in ourselves. We have no idea of the Supreme Being except what we learn from reflection on our own faculties. If our ignorance, therefore, were a good reason for rejecting anything, we should be led into the principle of denying all energy in the Supreme Being as much as in the grossest matter. We surely understand as little of the operations of the one as of the other. Is it more difficult to conceive that motion may arise from impact than that it may arise from volition? All we know is our profound ignorance in both cases[15].

[15] I need not examine at length the _vis inertiae_ so much talked of in the new philosophy, and ascribed to matter. We find by experience that a body at rest or in motion continues forever in its present state, until put from it by some new cause; and that a body struck takes as much motion from the striking body as it acquires itself. These are facts. When we call this a _vis inertiae_, we only mark these facts, without pretending to have any idea of the inert power; just as, when we talk of gravity, we mean certain effects, without comprehending that active power. It was never Sir Isaac Newton's meaning to strip second causes of all force or energy, though some of his followers have tried to establish that theory on his authority. On the contrary, that great philosopher had recourse to an etherial active fluid to explain his universal attraction, though he was so cautious and modest as to allow that it was a mere hypothesis, not to be insisted on without more experiments. I must admit that there is something a little extraordinary in the fate of opinions. Descartes hinted at the doctrine of the universal and sole efficacy of the Deity without insisting on it. Malebranche and the other Cartesians made it the foundation of all their philosophy. It had, however, no authority in England. Locke, Clarke, and Cudworth never so much as take notice of it, but suppose throughout that matter has a real, though subordinate and derived, power. By what means has it become so prevalent among our modern metaphysicians?

chapters.title: Section 7: OF THE IDEA OF NECESSARY CONNEXION. — Part 2
paragraphs: 58. But to hasten to a conclusion of this argument, which has already been drawn out at too great length: we have searched in vain for an idea of power or necessary connection in all the sources from which we might suppose it to be derived. It appears that, in single instances of the operation of bodies, we can never, by the utmost scrutiny, discover anything but one event following another, without being able to grasp any force or power by which the cause operates, or any connection between it and its supposed effect. The same difficulty arises in contemplating the operations of mind on body — where we observe the motion of the latter follow on the volition of the former, but are not able to observe or conceive the tie that binds motion and volition together, or the energy by which the mind produces this effect. The authority of the will over its own faculties and ideas is no more comprehensible. So that, on the whole, there does not appear in all nature one instance of connection that is conceivable to us. All events seem entirely loose and separate. One event follows another, but we can never observe any tie between them. They seem _conjoined_, but never _connected_. And since we can have no idea of anything that never appeared to our outward sense or inward sentiment, the necessary conclusion _seems_ to be that we have no idea of connection or power at all, and that these words are absolutely without meaning when used either in philosophical reasonings or in common life.

59. But there still remains one method of avoiding this conclusion, and one source we have not yet examined. When any natural object or event is presented, it is impossible for us, by any sagacity or insight, to discover, or even guess, without experience, what event will result from it, or to carry our foresight beyond the object immediately present to memory and senses. Even after one instance or experiment in which we have observed a particular event to follow upon another, we are not entitled to form a general rule, or to predict what will happen in similar cases — it being rightly considered an unpardonable rashness to judge the whole course of nature from a single experiment, however accurate or certain. But when one particular kind of event has, in every instance, always been conjoined with another, we no longer hesitate to predict the one upon the appearance of the other, and to employ that reasoning which alone can assure us of any matter of fact or existence. We then call the one object _Cause_, the other _Effect_. We suppose that there is some connection between them — some power in the one by which it infallibly produces the other, and operates with the greatest certainty and strongest necessity.

It appears, then, that this idea of a necessary connection among events arises from a number of similar instances of the constant conjunction of these events; nor can that idea ever be suggested by any one of these instances, surveyed in all possible lights and positions. But there is nothing in a number of instances, different from every single instance which is supposed to be exactly similar — except only that, after a repetition of similar instances, the mind is carried by habit, upon the appearance of one event, to expect its usual attendant, and to believe that it will exist. This connection, therefore, which we _feel_ in the mind, this customary transition of the imagination from one object to its usual attendant, is the sentiment or impression from which we form the idea of power or necessary connection. Nothing further is involved. Consider the subject from every side; you will never find any other origin for that idea. This is the sole difference between one instance, from which we can never derive the idea of connection, and a number of similar instances by which it is suggested. The first time a man saw the communication of motion by impact, as in the collision of two billiard balls, he could not pronounce that the one event was _connected_ with the other — only that it was _conjoined_ with it. After he has observed several instances of this nature, he then pronounces them to be _connected_. What change has happened to give rise to this new idea of _connection_? Nothing but this: he now _feels_ these events to be connected in his imagination, and can readily predict the existence of one from the appearance of the other. When we say, therefore, that one object is connected with another, we mean only that they have acquired a connection in our thought, and give rise to this inference by which they become proofs of each other's existence — a conclusion that is somewhat extraordinary, but seems founded on sufficient evidence. Nor will its evidence be weakened by any general distrust of the understanding, or skeptical suspicion of every conclusion that is new and extraordinary. No conclusions can be more agreeable to skepticism than those that make discoveries about the weakness and narrow limits of human reason and capacity.

60. And what stronger instance can be produced of the surprising ignorance and weakness of the understanding than the present one? For surely, if there is any relation among objects that it concerns us to know perfectly, it is that of cause and effect. On it are founded all our reasonings about matter of fact or existence. By it alone we attain any assurance about objects removed from the present testimony of memory and senses. The only immediate utility of all the sciences is to teach us how to control and regulate future events by their causes. Our thoughts and inquiries are therefore, at every moment, occupied with this relation. Yet so imperfect are the ideas we form of it that it is impossible to give any sound definition of cause, except one drawn from something extraneous and foreign to it. Similar objects are always conjoined with similar. Of this we have experience. In accordance with this experience, then, we may define a cause to be _an object, followed by another, and where all the objects similar to the first are followed by objects similar to the second_. Or, in other words, _where, if the first object had not been, the second would never have existed_. The appearance of a cause always conveys the mind, by a customary transition, to the idea of the effect. Of this also we have experience. We may therefore, in accordance with this experience, form another definition of cause, and call it _an object followed by another, and whose appearance always conveys the thought to that other_. But although both these definitions are drawn from circumstances foreign to the cause, we cannot remedy this inconvenience, or reach any more perfect definition that may point out that feature in the cause which gives it a connection with its effect. We have no idea of this connection, nor even any distinct notion of what it is we want to know when we attempt a conception of it. We say, for instance, that the vibration of this string is the cause of this particular sound. But what do we mean by that assertion? We either mean _that this vibration is followed by this sound, and that all similar vibrations have been followed by similar sounds_; or _that this vibration is followed by this sound, and that upon the appearance of one the mind anticipates the senses and immediately forms an idea of the other_. We may consider the relation of cause and effect in either of these two ways; but beyond these, we have no idea of it.[16]

[16] According to these explications and definitions, the idea of _power_ is just as relative as that of _cause_; and both refer to an effect, or some other event constantly conjoined with the former. When we consider the _unknown_ feature of an object by which the degree or quantity of its effect is fixed and determined, we call that its power; and accordingly, it is granted by all philosophers that the effect is the measure of the power. But if they had any idea of power as it is in itself, why could they not measure it in itself? The dispute over whether the force of a body in motion varies as its velocity, or as the square of its velocity, need not — I say — be decided by comparing its effects in equal or unequal times, but by a direct measurement and comparison.

As to the frequent use of the words Force, Power, Energy, etc., which occur everywhere in common conversation as well as in philosophy, that is no proof that we are acquainted, in any instance, with the connecting principle between cause and effect, or can ultimately account for the production of one thing by another. These words, as commonly used, have very loose meanings attached to them, and their ideas are very uncertain and confused. No animal can put external bodies in motion without the sentiment of a _nisus_ or endeavor; and every animal has a sentiment or feeling from the stroke or blow of an external object in motion. These sensations, which are merely animal, and from which we can _a priori_ draw no inference, we are apt to transfer to inanimate objects, and to suppose that they have some such feelings whenever they transfer or receive motion. As to energies that are exerted without our attaching to them any idea of communicated motion, we consider only the constant experienced conjunction of the events; and since we _feel_ a customary connection between the ideas, we transfer that feeling to the objects, as nothing is more usual than to apply to external bodies every internal sensation they cause.

61. To summarize, then, the reasonings of this section: every idea is copied from some preceding impression or sentiment; and where we cannot find any impression, we may be certain that there is no idea. In all single instances of the operation of bodies or minds, there is nothing that produces any impression, nor consequently can suggest any idea of power or necessary connection. But when many uniform instances appear, and the same object is always followed by the same event, we then begin to entertain the notion of cause and connection. We then _feel_ a new sentiment or impression — namely, a customary connection in thought or imagination between one object and its usual attendant — and this sentiment is the original of the idea we are looking for. For since this idea arises from a number of similar instances, and not from any single instance, it must arise from that feature in which the number of instances differs from every individual instance. But this customary connection or transition of the imagination is the only feature in which they differ. In every other respect they are alike. The first instance we saw of motion communicated by the impact of two billiard balls (to return to this obvious illustration) is exactly similar to any instance that may presently occur to us, except only that we could not, at first, _infer_ one event from the other, which we can now do, after so long a course of uniform experience. I do not know whether the reader will readily grasp this reasoning. I am afraid that if I multiplied words about it, or threw it into a greater variety of lights, it would only become more obscure and intricate. In all abstract reasonings there is one point of view which, if we can happily hit upon it, will go further toward illustrating the subject than all the eloquence and copious expression in the world. This point of view we should try to reach, and reserve the flowers of rhetoric for subjects more suited to them.
